data.summary: A Thunderbolt device you approve can read and write all of the computer's memory. Only approve Thunderbolt devices you trust. USB-C hubs and screens are not affected.

details.what: The firmware does not ask the kernel for Kernel DMA Protection (no DMAR platform opt-in), and the kernel does not turn the IOMMU on by itself (CONFIG_INTEL_IOMMU_DEFAULT_ON unset, no intel_iommu=on). So the IOMMU stays off: /sys/class/iommu is empty, there are no IOMMU groups, and the Thunderbolt domain reports iommu_dma_protection=0.
details.attack: A Thunderbolt PCIe device that gets approved, or one that copies the identity of an approved device (the Thunderspy class), can read and write all memory by DMA: passwords, disk keys, the running kernel. It needs physical access to a USB-C port. The domain's security level still makes a new device wait for approval first.
details.fix: Turn the IOMMU on with the kernel option intel_iommu=on, as a per-model quirk proven by its own evidence (it can affect the discrete GPU driver, suspend and other PCIe devices). Until then, approve only trusted Thunderbolt devices.
details.when: Testing intel_iommu=on needs a reboot of each affected model.
details.check: cat /sys/bus/thunderbolt/devices/domain0/iommu_dma_protection (the controller may need a device plugged in or force_power to appear); ls /sys/class/iommu
details.references: fwupd HSI attributes org.fwupd.hsi.Iommu and pre-boot DMA protection (https://fwupd.github.io/libfwupdplugin/hsi.html); Thunderspy (https://thunderspy.io); kernel Thunderbolt security levels (https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/thunderbolt.html)

zbookX2G4Measured.reason: Measured on the HP ZBook x2 G4 (BIOS P72 01.53, kernel 7.2.2, JHL6540 Alpine Ridge): with force_power on, domain0 security=secure, iommu_dma_protection=0, no boot_acl; no iommu option on the command line, /sys/class/iommu empty, 0 IOMMU groups.
